CLAUDE_101.TITLE: Beyond code: Learning to collaborate with AI
CLAUDE_101.CONTENT:
How can I integrate AI without losing control?

As a recent DAW graduate, one of the questions I ask myself most is: how can I integrate AI without losing control or the quality of what I build? I don't want AI to write everything for me; I want it to be a partner that helps me be more efficient without hindering my learning process.

Last week, I completed Anthropic's Claude 101 course, and the experience changed my mindset. It's not just about asking a chat questions, but about understanding how to structure context so the output is truly useful.

What I take away from this training

What surprised me most was the management of Projects and Artifacts. Until now, I saw prompts as isolated things. But by treating the 'Project' as a context database and the 'Artifact' as a presentation layer to render code, the interaction becomes much more logical and professional.

Another key point is the potential of Skills and automation. I am already preparing a custom skill to review my own code under Clean Code standards. I find it fascinating to be able to turn repetitive tasks into automatic processes.

Finally, the use of Claude Code in the terminal has been a discovery. Being able to integrate a local development agent makes a real difference in daily productivity.

What's next?

This is just the first step. I am convinced that a developer's value lies not only in writing code, but in knowing how to orchestrate the right tools to solve complex problems cleanly.

I am going to turn this space into a log of my technical learnings. The goal is simple: to grow, share what works, and, above all, to keep learning.

PANTRYCHEF_DB.TITLE: PantryChef: Designing the database before writing a single line of code
PANTRYCHEF_DB.CONTENT:
Starting with design, not code

After finishing my Higher Degree in Web Application Development (DAW), I decided to start a new personal project: PantryChef, a full-stack application aimed at helping manage ingredients in the pantry and suggesting recipes based on what the user actually has.

The first temptation when starting a project is usually to open the IDE and create the first controller or component. However, this time I wanted to do it differently. Before writing a single line of code in Spring Boot or Angular, I am dedicating time to understanding the problem domain and designing the database correctly.

Ultimately, an application is nothing more than a representation of a real-world problem. If the data model is poorly planned from the start, the entire architecture will end up carrying the weight of those decisions.

Understanding the domain before modeling it

During this first phase, I am not thinking about tables or SQL queries. I am trying to answer much more important questions:

  • What information does the application really need to store?
  • Which data belongs to the user and which is part of the system's catalog?
  • What are the relationships between ingredients and recipes?
  • What information changes over time and what remains stable?

Answering these questions has allowed me to identify the main elements of the domain: users, ingredients, recipes, and each user's personal pantry. From them, the real modeling work begins.

An MVP with room to grow

One of the most important decisions was to limit the scope of the first version. Instead of trying to design a massive database from the start, I chose to build a solid, well-structured MVP.

This first version will consist only of the essential entities:

  • User.
  • Ingredient.
  • Ingredient Category.
  • Unit of Measurement.
  • Recipe.
  • Recipe Ingredients.
  • Ingredients stored by each user in their pantry.

This approach allows for developing all core functionalities without introducing unnecessary complexity. Furthermore, it leaves the foundation ready to incorporate future features like shopping lists, weekly planning, favorites, or nutritional information without needing to redesign the model.

The importance of proper normalization

One of my personal goals for this project is to correctly apply the database design concepts learned during my studies.

Instead of storing repeated information across multiple tables, the model aims for each piece of data to exist in only one place and exactly where it belongs. To achieve this, I am applying the first three normal forms (1NF, 2NF, and 3NF), eliminating redundancies and separating responsibilities between entities.

For example, an ingredient exists only once in the entire database. It is then reused by both recipes and each user's pantry. Similarly, units of measurement are managed as an independent catalog, avoiding inconsistencies and facilitating future expansions.

These decisions may seem small at first, but they are what allow an application to remain maintainable as it begins to grow.

Beyond the ERD

During this process, I've realized that designing a database consists of much more than drawing an Entity-Relationship Diagram.

Each relationship responds to a business need, each entity has a concrete responsibility, and each decision involves weighing different alternatives. It is as much an exercise in analysis and architecture as it is in data modeling.

This preliminary work also greatly facilitates subsequent development with Spring Boot and JPA/Hibernate, as the domain entities faithfully reflect the model designed during this phase.

What's next?

This article marks the beginning of the PantryChef project. In future posts, I will document how the development evolves, from the detailed design of the ERD to its implementation with Spring Boot, the construction of the REST API, and the integration with Angular.

My goal is not only to build a functional application but to document every technical decision, explain why it was made, and turn the project into an opportunity to continue learning and sharing that knowledge with other developers.
